The NBS will overhaul its survey methods by adopting big data, cloud computing and AI to boost ‘efficiency and scientific rigour’
China’s National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) has been tasked with uncovering fabricated data using modern technology, according to the latest update to the agency’s responsibilities endorsed by Beijing.
On Friday, the State Commission Office for Public Sector Reform published a revised scheme dictating the agency’s functions, internal structure and staffing quotas.

articles.title_orig: Saudi Aramco Tower Damaged as Yemen’s Houthis Attack Riyadh
articles.title_zh: Saudi Aramco Tower Damaged as Yemen’s Houthis Attack Riyadh
articles.content_orig:
A building belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco in the financial district of the capital Riyadh has been damaged in a missile attack.
The strike in King Abdullah Financial District has been claimed by the Iran-allied Houthis and came after Saudi Civil Defense issued ‌an early-warning ⁠alert of a potential threat to the city.
Video circulating on social media and verified by CNN shows damage to several floors of the Aramco building, with windows seen blown out. But Saudi authorities said the impact was minimal.
“An administrative building belonging to Saudi Aramco in Riyadh was subjected to an attempted attack,” on Sunday, according to the official Saudi news agency, citing a source at the Saudi Energy Ministry.
“The incident resulted in falling shrapnel that caused minor damage to the building, with no injuries or fatalities reported,” the agency reported.
However, one witness said they saw ambulances heading to the area.
CNN has reached out to the Information Ministry by email for further details.
The Houthis, who have fired missiles and drones towards multiple targets across Saudi Arabia over the last three months, said in the attack on Riyadh’s financial district was one of several it carried out on Aramco targets. There was no initial comment from Saudi authorities on the additional claims.
The Houthis said they had also targeted Saudi-led ground forces in several parts of Yemen.
The Saudi led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed two cruise missiles in Riyadh and the southern region. Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki wrote in a post on X that air defenses also “intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh.”
The missile attacks on Riyadh came a day after Yemen’s Houthi-run health ministry said Saudi airstrikes had ‌killed ‌at least ​33 ​people near the capital Sanaa, including women and children.
“We will punish the Saudi regime for its crimes against the Yemeni people,” said Mahdi al-Mashat, a senior Houthi official, on Saturday.
Last month, 13 people were killed in one missile strike on Riyadh’s international airport, and several more died in other strikes on the airport.
The Houthis have said they will continue firing missiles and drones against Saudi Arabia so long as the Kingdom carries out airstrikes against the parts of Yemen they control and enforces a blockade against its territory.
Saudi Arabia spent $83 billion on defense last year, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, putting it firmly among the top ten military spenders worldwide. It has acquired US fighter jets as well as Patriot and THAAD air defense systems, and a range of advanced weaponry from France and the United Kingdom.
But the Saudis have a lot to defend: a country roughly one-fifth the size of the US, with threats on three sides - from Iran , Iranian-backed militias in Iraq, and the Houthis.
Iran’s hardliners see a weakened Trump – and want more to end the war
The Saudis are intercepting many of the missiles and drones fired by the Houthis. But some get through . The defense ministry faces difficult choices in distributing the existing systems with so many installations vulnerable to attack.
The Houthis have learned to combine ballistic and cruise missiles with long-range drones to overwhelm Saudi defenses, according to analysts.
In Yemen, the Saudi-backed coalition is trying to prevent the Houthis from advancing further south towards the port of Aden, which is held by the internationally-recognized government.
The Houthis have frequently targeted Aden’s airport with missiles in recent weeks, after taking a stretch of Yemen’s Red Sea coast in September.
Hostilities between the Houthis, who are backed by Iran, and Saudi Arabia reignited in July, shattering a 2022 UN-brokered ceasefire that had largely halted fighting ⁠between the ‌two sides.
Ibrahim Dahman, Teele Rebane and Farida Elsebai contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Trump unveils 'Iron Gate' task force against Iran as Saudis launch deadly strikes on Houthi rebels
articles.title_zh: Trump unveils 'Iron Gate' task force against Iran as Saudis launch deadly strikes on Houthi rebels
articles.content_orig:
Secretary of War Pete Hegseth is facing a bipartisan impeachment threat when Congress returns next week as Republicans seethe over their devastating losses in Tuesday's midterm elections.
Bipartisan frustration over the war in Iran, quietly simmering for months, is now openly erupting after Democrats stunned the country with historic victories in the House and Senate. That anger could all now hit Hegseth, with several House Republicans telling Fox News Digital that they believe a resolution to impeach him could pass as early as next week.
"He's screwed," one House GOP lawmaker told Fox News Digital.
Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., a longtime critic of foreign intervention by the U.S., told Fox News Digital he intends to force a vote on impeaching Hegseth when Congress returns if the Pentagon chief does not resign first.
He'll do so by filing a privileged resolution, a mechanism aimed at getting a vote on legislation despite opposition from the majority party's leaders. Once a privileged resolution is filed, lawmakers have two legislative days to hold a vote.
But the procedure notably carries two steps. Before a vote on the measure itself, leaders can call up a vote to "table" the bill or refer it to the relevant committee, which in both instances effectively kills it.
That procedural vote is normally where most privileged resolutions die. But in this case, several House Republicans told Fox News Digital they believe the impeachment resolution could ultimately be successful.
This is an excerpt from an article by Fox News' Liz Elkind.
Former CIA Station Chief Dan Hoffman joins Jon Scott to analyze the shifting political coalition in Israel and Donald Trump's confirmation of a military strike on an Iranian anti-aircraft device.
Hoffman remains skeptical that the U.S. and Iran will come to a negotiated settlement in the near future.
Trump has not ruled out a return to full scale war.
California Post opinion editor Joel Pollak discussed how the Iran war and President Donald Trump’s actions influenced voter sentiment in the 2026 midterm elections on ‘Life, Liberty & Levin.’
While Pollak acknowledged that the war had a negative impact of Republicans in the midterms, he argued that Americans will be grateful for Trump's actions down the line.
DUBAI, United Arab Emirates — A senior United Arab Emirates official says he is cautiously optimistic about negotiations between the United States and Iran, citing progress through Qatari mediation over the past days, even as fears of renewed military confrontation continue to grip the Middle East.
"We see some progress. … We hope that both sides will be able to reach a point where they will start building trust and engaging in a way to avoid the war, to find a political solution. … I am a little bit optimistic, but I don't exclude the other option," Dr. Ali Rashid Al Nuaimi, chairman of the Defense, Interior and Foreign Affairs Committee of the UAE's Federal National Council, told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview.
His remarks came as Reuters reported Nov. 5 that Iran had submitted a new nuclear proposal to Washington through Qatar.
Tehran, however, continued to insist that the U.S. meet seven conditions before negotiations could proceed, including sanctions relief and an end to the American naval blockade.
President Donald Trump has not ruled out further military operations, while Iran has threatened broader retaliation if fighting resumes.
For the UAE, which endured thousands of Iranian missile and drone attacks earlier this year, the possibility of a diplomatic breakthrough offers hope. But its leaders are making clear that hope cannot replace preparedness.
"We plan for the worst. We hope for the best. … We always make sure that we are ready to deal with all the challenges or the threats," Al Nuaimi said.That combination of optimism and caution was evident during Fox News Digital's reporting trip across the Emirates, where daily life appeared remarkably normal despite the uncertainty surrounding the country.
On an evening in downtown Dubai, restaurant terraces were packed, tourists filled the streets and crowds gathered around a fountain show set to music that moved between Arabic songs and Western pop hits.
This is an excerpt from an article by Fox News' Efrat Lachter.
The U.S. announced Task Force Iron Gate on Saturday, which is meant to track illegal movement of advanced weapons, dual-use technologies, illegal revenue streams and other sanctioned material over Iran’s border and the Caspian Sea as the U.S. expands its naval blockade.
The task force will be based in Tampa and coordinate with several U.S. agencies.
The new effort comes in addition to the U.S. blockade on Iranian ports.
U.S. forces disabled a commercial vessel that attempted to violate the blockade in the Gulf of Oman on Saturday, CENTCOM said, adding that the vessel ignored repeated warnings.
A U.S. military aircraft disabled the St. Kitts-flagged M/V Huda by firing munitions at its stern.
“CENTCOM continues to strictly enforce America’s naval blockade against Iran,” CENTCOM said in a release. “Enforcement actions since July have resulted in U.S. forces redirecting 147 commercial vessels that complied and disabled five merchant ships that refused to comply.”
CENTCOM added that the U.S. has also destroyed 10 Iranian commercial oil tankers that were part of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps’ multibillion-dollar shadow network.
Fox News' Brie Stimson contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Russia targets emergency crews at the site of a deadly strike in southern Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Russia targets emergency crews at the site of a deadly strike in southern Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine – There are only eight people left in Volodymyr’s village. That was the last count he remembers before deciding to leave.
“We were in the cellar when they started bombing us with drones,” he said, nervously rubbing his red, blistered hands together. “As you can see, I was completely burned.”
Last week, he fled his home in Preobrazhenka, just over 40km (25 miles) from where he now sits in a shelter for displaced people in the regional capital, Zaporizhzhia.
The villages south of Zaporizhzhia have been coming under escalating Russian attacks.
On November 2, in one of this year’s deadliest attacks in Ukraine, nine Russian glide bombs struck the town of Komyshuvakha , killing at least 50 people. Many had gathered to receive humanitarian aid at a local school. Several people are still missing, feared dead under the rubble.
The constant threat of bombs and drones makes everyday life almost unbearable.
Over the past three years, this war has proven that an army no longer needs boots on the ground.
The arrival of Russian First-Person-View (FPV) drones overhead is often a sign of the Russian infantry’s gradual advance. Well-documented footage shows these drones deliberately targeting vehicles and civilians on the streets. Ukrainians say drones have stalked civilians in cities including Kherson , Kramatorsk and Sloviansk.
Now, Zaporizhzhia is showing some of the same warning signs.
The city administration is doing what it can to protect residents, installing anti-drone netting over streets and civilian infrastructure in the Cosmos neighbourhood. But boarded-up windows and bombed-out buildings across the city show how difficult it is to mitigate the threat once the drones arrive.
Denys Knysh, a regional military administration official, says authorities are preparing to relocate the shelter where Volodymyr is staying to another neighbourhood “if the situation gets worse”.
Many in the shelter are elderly or have limited mobility. Some lack the documents they need to relocate, making evacuation more difficult.
Others prefer to stay in Zaporizhzhia, close to their former homes, holding on to hope that the war will end and they can return.
Since the beginning of the war, Zaporizhzhia has provided refuge for thousands of internally displaced people fleeing Russia’s occupation. People have arrived from cities like Mariupol and Melitopol, which fell under Russian control early in the conflict.
Now, as the security situation deteriorates, some of those who once fled to Zaporizhzhia for safety face the prospect of having to leave again.
Alina, who works in a flower shop beneath protective drone netting, said, “Of course I may have to leave, but I don’t want to.”
She hears the buzz of Russian drones almost every day.
Nearby, along the Pryberezhna Highway that follows the river, every petrol station and business is covered in the protective netting.
“It’s scary and dangerous, everything is flying around. Just today a drone flew over us,” said Nataliia, an employee at a petrol station.
Earlier that day, Russian Banderol missiles, a type of low-cost, jet-powered cruise missile, struck a shopping mall and the main bridge into the city. An FPV drone also hit a city bus.
Zaporizhzhia still has signs of normality. Twinkling lights hang over restaurant terraces and some streets still buzz with life.
But the transition is rarely clear-cut.
People gradually adapt to each new threat. It starts with streets covered in nets. Then drone jammers on the roofs of city buses. Bridges bear gaping holes from attacks. Children walk around carrying drone detectors.
Knysh says authorities are ready to evacuate the city if and when that time comes.
“It’s very difficult to calculate [how many people are left in the city] because every day people leave Zaporizhzhia,” he told Al Jazeera. “The demographic in Google doesn’t correspond to the reality.”

articles.title_orig: I lost my tech job and couldn't afford my mortgage. Now I live in a 100-square-foot shed in the yard.
articles.title_zh: I lost my tech job and couldn't afford my mortgage. Now I live in a 100-square-foot shed in the yard.
articles.content_orig:
This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Lauren Patton, 36, who built a tiny home in her Texas backyard. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity.
After a couple of years of living in Chicago, I decided to move back to Texas and get a fresh start. This was in 2022, when the real estate market was booming, and homes in Central Texas were getting bought up quickly.
I found a real estate agent on Instagram, and she helped me buy a small bungalow — two bedrooms and about 1,000 square feet — for about $400,000. I was buying alone; it was just me and my dog.
I had made a very small down payment on my home and taken out a 30-year mortgage. My monthly payment was about $4,000, which was a lot at first, but I thought it was affordable given my well-paying job.
At the time, I was working in tech and doing really well. I had been moving up the data science ladder, and I thought it would be a lucrative field. But I was a bit wrong about that.
In early 2023, there were a bunch of tech layoffs . I found out the day after I got back from a trip to South Africa that I had been let go. I was given only two months of severance and sent on my way.
For the first couple of months after I was laid off , I was OK. I took time to relax, spent time with my family, and did the things you don't get to do while you're working. Then I started looking for jobs.
I wasn't super worried at first. I thought, "Hey, I was a data science manager. I'll be able to find something." But after interviewing at numerous places, nothing was happening.
By then, money was tight. I had very little savings and was still paying off a lot of credit card debt. I filed for unemployment, which brought in some money, and started renting out my home on Airbnb to help cover my mortgage.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
To make this work, I rented a room for myself across town for about six months. But when my unemployment ran out, I had to start crashing on people's couches and driving for Lyft— basically doing whatever I could.
In 2024, I reached out to a former boss and asked if I could get my previous accounting job back. I did, and while it paid much less than I was making before, it sustained me for a while.
Still, I had no savings, and I had cashed out my 401(k) . I was terrified. My mortgage was just so much; I thought my home was going to go into foreclosure. I was already about 30% underwater on the home, and it had depreciated in value, so I still didn't want to sell.
I was 35 and thought, "I can't keep doing this." I knew I needed to do something. That's when I came up with the idea to build a little structure in my backyard to live in.
I wasn't confident enough in my woodworking or carpentry skills, so I decided to buy a cabin-style shed kit I found out about on Instagram. I took out a loan and bought it for about $8,500.
While I was building the shed , I moved back into my main house and got a roommate to help cover the mortgage. I charged about $1,200 a month for the room. It wasn't a huge portion of my mortgage payment, but it helped. Looking back, I regret buying a two-bedroom house, because there just aren't enough bedrooms to rent out.
The shed is about 100 square feet, and the kit came with stackable wood slats, beams, and big windows, but it didn't include a roof or a floor. I had to build the foundation , too. I also added an outhouse with an outdoor shower and built fences and other things around the property.
For the construction, I relied on YouTube and ChatGPT — though ChatGPT definitely led me astray on a few things, especially the roofing.
I officially finished the build in March 2025, though I've been making adjustments ever since — it's never-ending.
Since moving into the shed, I've been renting out my main home full-time on Airbnb and have hosted hundreds of guests.
I let Airbnb handle the pricing. On a typical weekend night, I charge around $200; on a weekday during the school year, it's closer to $125.
October is especially lucrative because of the Austin City Limits music festival. This October, my home had about 96% occupancy, and my gross earnings were about $6,516.70. That's not normal — occupancy and nightly rates were higher — but Airbnb deducted $619 in service fees. I also had the home cleaned seven times for about $100 each time.
I put some of the money I earned toward my mortgage and bills for the shed — my total electric bill, including the shed and the house, is $550, which also includes other utilities.
But overall, Airbnb doesn't cover my full mortgage, which increased by $400 a month this year because of home insurance.
It was tough at first, downsizing to a tiny home . Emotionally, it felt like I was regressing in life, and physically, it felt really claustrophobic. But I don't mind it as much now. I'm doing better mentally.
I have most of what I need in a normal house — a TV, a desk, and a bed. But I have a tiny, itty-bitty fridge, and I don't have ice or running water, so I have to stock up on jugs of water.
I've had to learn a lot about how to live in the space . When I first moved in, I had a portable air conditioner, and the humidity would reach 80%. I'd wake up soaking wet and think, "What's going on?" I'd never had to consider something like that before. Now, I run a dehumidifier 24 hours a day.
The hardest part is remembering to keep everything I need on hand, because there's always one thing missing. I'll go to grill chicken and realize I'm out of salt, or that it's back in the main house. I'm constantly running out to buy little things, and sometimes I wonder whether it's really financially worth it.
Some days, I think, "Man, this is harder than I thought it was going to be."
At this point, I've tried literally everything I can do to keep my home — I mean everything. If things don't get better in the next couple of years, I'll be comfortable letting it go, because I know I tried my hardest.
Looking back, I wish I had done more research as a first-time homebuyer . Aside from a high mortgage, my house is also like 100 years old, so it often needs repairs. I thought I was handy and could do it all myself, but it really wears on your soul.
I also wish I had thought more about the financial worst-case scenario. You hear advice from your parents: Don't let your mortgage take up too much of your income. I wish I had listened and hadn't gone over that 30% threshold .
The next time I buy a home, I need to stay under it. I also can't be so optimistic. I need to be more realistic, because this has shifted my life so much.
A couple of weeks ago, I started posting about my layoff and the shed on social media. It's really taken off; I've gained around 12,000 followers on Instagram .
I'm really grateful. Most people have been so great and lovely. And while I haven't earned any money from my reels yet, I'm working on it.
As for a job, I'm currently working on a data analytics project and am still walking dogs. My income from my jobs doesn't cover my mortgage, but I'm just grateful to have a job at all.
I feel sorry for people getting laid off, and I can definitely relate. When I'm back on my feet and in a better place financially, I want to help as many people in similar situations as I can.
One day, I'd like to move back into the main house and rent out the shed for a few hundred dollars to someone who needs an affordable place to live.

articles.title_orig: Will Eisenkot be able to form Israel’s next gov’t amid divided opposition?
articles.title_zh: Will Eisenkot be able to form Israel’s next gov’t amid divided opposition?
articles.content_orig:
Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has been given the opportunity to form a new government after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s ruling coalition lost its parliamentary majority in the October elections, raising the possibility of an end to his long tenure in power.
President Isaac Herzog selected the former military chief on Saturday, following consultations with political parties. Eisenkot has 28 days to cobble together a coalition to form a government. If he fails to form a new administration within that period, he can seek a 14-day extension.
“Now is the time to form a national emergency government. I will do everything to ensure we are worthy,” Eisenkot, the leader of the Yashar party, posted on X.
However, the 66-year-old faces a difficult challenge as many of the opposition parties hold sharply conflicting positions on national security, religion and the Israeli occupation of Palestinian territory.
Neither Eisenkot nor Netanyahu has a 61-seat majority in Israel’s 120-member parliament, the Knesset.
As a result, Arab-led parties hold a potentially decisive role in determining who governs Israel, even as Eisenkot and his prospective partners refuse to rely on their support.
So what do we now know about Eisenkot’s possible paths to power, and can he succeed in unseating Netanyahu?
Eisenkot’s potential coalition spans his Yashar party, the centre-left Democrats led by Yair Golan, Naftali Bennett’s centre-right Together party and Avigdor Lieberman’s right-wing Yisrael Beiteinu (Israel Our Home).
Overall, they control 48 seats, well short of a majority.
Arab-led parties Ra’am (United List) and the Joint List (comprising three parties – Hadash, Ta’al and Balad) – jointly holding 19 seats – have endorsed Eisenkot’s attempt to form a government. Their backing would give the broader anti-Netanyahu camp a combined 67 seats.
Hadash is an Arab-Jewish party, Ta’al advocates for the rights of Palestinian citizens of Israel, and Balad demands equal rights for all its citizens.
However, Eisenkot has ruled out bringing Arab parties into his government, while Lieberman has repeatedly rejected forming a minority administration dependent on their support. Golan’s Democrats have been more willing to partner with Ra’am and the Joint List.
“We must no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes,” Golan said after the election.
Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist coalition has fallen from the 64 seats it secured in 2022 to 53, eight seats short of a majority.
His Likud is the largest individual party with 27 seats, while Eisenkot’s Yashar won 21.
Netanyahu’s efforts to remain in power suffered a further setback when United Torah Judaism, a longtime ultra-Orthodox ally, declined to endorse him or any other candidate during consultations with Herzog.
While the decision hurts Netanyahu’s prospects of regaining power, it did not rule out the party supporting him in future coalition negotiations if their demands were met, particularly compulsory military service for ultra-Orthodox Jews, which they reject.
If Eisenkot is unable to put together a coalition, he could potentially lead a minority government backed by Arab parties from outside.
A minority government is formed when the parties holding cabinet positions do not collectively control a majority of seats in parliament. Instead, they depend on support from lawmakers outside the governing coalition to remain in power and pass legislation.
Eisenkot could establish such an administration with his four-party bloc relying on external parliamentary support from Ra’am and the Joint List .
Under this arrangement, the Arab-led parties would not necessarily receive cabinet positions or formally join the coalition.
They could instead negotiate policy concessions in exchange for their parliamentary support.
In 2021, Ra’am joined a government led by Bennett, becoming the first independent Arab party to participate in an Israeli governing coalition.
That administration collapsed after 18 months, mainly due to disagreements over the illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank and Palestinian statehood. Most Israeli parties do not support the creation of a sovereign Palestinian state as part of the so-called two-state solution.
Netanyahu, who has been in power for most of the past 20 years, has openly rejected Palestinian statehood and has pushed settlement expansions that are the biggest hurdles in the realisation of Palestinian statehood. Settlements are considered illegal under international law.
Beyond a minority government, Eisenkot could attempt to secure a parliamentary majority by bringing Israel’s two ultra-Orthodox parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism, into his coalition.
Together, they hold 13 seats, which would give Eisenkot’s bloc exactly the 61 seats required for a majority.
However, such an alliance would require compromises over military conscription exemptions for ultra-Orthodox religious students, an issue that has long divided Israeli politics.
Eisenkot and his allies, particularly Lieberman, have criticised the exemptions. But Lieberman has recently indicated that he is open to compromise.
While United Torah Judaism has refused to endorse Netanyahu, Shas backed the beleaguered prime minister.
Another option would be a unity government involving Eisenkot’s Yashar, Bennett’s Together party, Lieberman’s Israel Our Home and Netanyahu’s Likud.
Such an alliance would command 67 seats, but would require Eisenkot and his partners to abandon their central election pledge to remove Netanyahu from power.
If Eisenkot fails to form a government within the required time, Herzog could give Netanyahu an opportunity to form a governing coalition.
Should both leaders fail, parliament could nominate another candidate. If no government emerges after a process lasting 100 days, Israelis could be heading to the polls again.
The negotiations could determine not only who becomes Israel’s next prime minister, but also which political parties control key ministries and shape policies on the economy, military conscription and the occupied Palestinian territory.
Several members of Eisenkot’s opposition bloc have previously held senior government positions, including in the coalition that removed Netanyahu from power in 2021.
Bennett, who served as prime minister from 2021 to 2022, has long opposed the establishment of a Palestinian state and advocated annexing large parts of the occupied West Bank.
During Israel’s 11-day war on Gaza in May 2021, Bennett, then an opposition politician, backed Netanyahu’s military offensive in the Palestinian enclave. More than 250 Palestinians were killed in Israeli attacks.
Meanwhile, Lieberman served as finance minister in Bennett’s government and previously held the defence portfolio under Netanyahu.
He previously proposed swapping some Arab communities in Israel proper for Jewish settlements in the occupied West Bank in the context of a final peace deal with the Palestinians.
Lieberman’s party backs illegal settlement expansion, including E1, and annexing all of Area C, 60 percent of the occupied West Bank already under full Israeli control. E1, which stands for East 1 settlement, is a 12sq km corridor with thousands of housing units. It will cut the West Bank into two parts.
Eisenkot himself served in Netanyahu’s wartime cabinet before leaving the government after disagreements over the conduct of the genocide in Gaza. He has not opposed the genocide but criticised Netanyahu for prioritising his political survival over security considerations.

Who is winning the AI race between the United States and China? The answer depends on what you measure.
Photo: Jason Edwards/Getty
Asia Power Snapshot: China, the United States, and the race for AI dominance
US President Donald Trump has declared that “whoever wins AI wins,” suggesting that the competition for mastery over artificial intelligence (AI) is the pre-eminent geopolitical contest of the day. But who is winning the AI race between the United States and China? The answer depends on what you measure. This Data Snapshot compares the inputs and outputs that matter most — from chips and compute to research and innovation — to show which side holds the lead, where the gaps are narrowing, and where capabilities may be overstated.
Based on a thorough analysis of available data, including 14 indicators across four measures — Resources, Technology, AI capabilities, and AI adoption — the United States is currently leading the race. However, its lead is far from uniform, and the competition remains uneven across multiple domains. The United States is well ahead in AI capabilities, driven by its dominance in compute, and in AI adoption, where its lead in web traffic and apps outweighs China’s edge in open models. By contrast, China has a clear lead in Resources, particularly critical minerals — the key materials needed for manufacturing the advanced technologies that make AI possible. Governance, however, remains contested. Neither superpower is widely trusted to regulate AI, leaving room for middle powers such as Australia to help shape the rules.
China holds a clear advantage over the United States in both production and known reserves of critical minerals.
In November 2025, the US Department of the Interior released a list of 60 minerals critical to its economic and national security interests. 1 China leads in production of 30, while the United States is ahead in only eight — with 22 not produced in either country. China holds larger known reserves of 20 listed minerals, and the United States of seven, with one tied, and insufficient data for the remaining 32.
China’s ability to impose targeted export controls on critical minerals poses a major risk for the United States. In 2023, Beijing began announcing restrictions on several, including gallium and germanium — both used in semiconductors. 2
To counter this vulnerability, the United States has sought to cooperate with other countries to secure critical minerals. It has developed Pax Silica, a 24-member international framework focused on AI-related supply chain resilience. 3 In Asia, it has critical minerals frameworks with Australia and Japan and has also signed memoranda of understanding with Malaysia and Thailand. 4 In February 2026, it held a Critical Minerals Ministerial meeting, where it signed an additional 11 bilateral agreements, including one with the Philippines. 5
* For more on the semiconductor supply chain in Asia, and Southeast Asia’s role as a connector between the United States and China, see Between the superpowers: Southeast Asia’s strategic supply chain dilemma (Opens in new window) .
The United States leads China in technological sophistication. While China has almost 11 million full-time equivalent researchers — over seven million more than the United States — US spending on research and development (R&D) is considerably higher as a share of GDP (3.45 per cent versus China’s 2.58 per cent). The United States also has a sizeable lead in the number of data centres and supercomputers.
The United States has sought to limit China’s access to advanced technologies that could help develop its semiconductor industry. Washington has imposed numerous restrictions on both China and Chinese subsidiaries abroad, which has, in turn, spurred affected companies to innovate around them. 6 In May 2026, Huawei announced a new chip-design approach intended to increase transistor density without shrinking transistors. This could allow it to design chips by 2031 with transistor density equivalent to that of the chips Taiwan’s TSMC aims to make in 2028, without the advanced lithography machines China is barred from importing. 7 If successful, this could limit the effect of US export controls.
While companies have looked for ways to work around US controls, Beijing has moved to expand its own, building on its critical mineral restrictions. In October 2026, China proposed adding 40 technologies to its restricted exports, including 23 related to AI — among them AI chip design, the core technology of the most advanced models, and AI tools, such as deepfake detection systems. 8
The United States maintains a lead in AI capabilities. Its AI data centres have nearly 40 times the combined computing power of China’s, and its AI chips 31 times. This has helped US models stay ahead in benchmark tests, though the margin is narrowing.
As of November 2026, the top US large language model (LLM) on Arena, a platform that ranks models through blind head-to-head comparisons, is Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon, with an estimated score of 1528, closely followed by Google’s Gemini 4 Argon at 1520 and Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 at 1509. China’s top model, Moonshot’s Kimi K3, released in mid-July 2026, scores an estimated 1488, placing it 19th. The last top US model at this level was Google’s Gemini 3 Pro, which led from its release in mid-November 2025 until late January 2026. This gap is consistent with claims that the United States has a six-to-nine-month lead in AI capabilities. 9
The global spread of LLMs is arguably the most important front in the AI race. The models that consumers, businesses, and governments rely on will shape the information they see, how their economies run, and, potentially, the future of war. Which country leads depends on how users access the models.
There are six main ways to do so:
Reliable data exist for four of these: websites, apps, self-hosted open models, and aggregator platforms.
China holds a comfortable lead in self-hosted open models and aggregator platforms. 10 In the third quarter of 2026, Chinese models were downloaded nearly 1.8 billion times on Hugging Face, compared with 500 million for US models, giving China 78 per cent of the two countries’ combined downloads. Such models particularly appeal to governments and businesses, which can run them on their own servers to keep data local and adapt them to their needs. On aggregator platform OpenRouter, Chinese models accounted for 55 per cent of all text requests in the week commencing 26 October 2026 — compared to the US share of 38 per cent.
However, most users access LLMs through websites, apps, and embedded AI. The United States has a commanding lead in websites and apps. US models drew more than 90 per cent of combined global traffic to US and Chinese AI websites. US models also accounted for more than 80 per cent of combined use of US and Chinese AI apps, based on Google Play downloads and, for China, where Google Play is unavailable, QuestMobile data.
Overall, most people who use AI rely on US models, giving the United States unmatched reach and greater influence over the technology’s global direction.
With no other country posing a challenge to their dominance in AI, the United States and China have an outsized influence over how the technology is governed globally.
Rival blocs are already taking shape. Washington launched Pax Silica in December 2025 to secure AI supply chains among trusted partners. Beijing answered in July 2026 with the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO), which centres on AI governance standards and digital development. Hundreds of thousands of people were left without power after Russian strikes hit Ukraine's energy infrastructure, authorities said on Sunday.
In the central Dnipropetrovsk region, "more than 600,000 residents of the region have been left without power," power company DTEK said on Telegram after a "night attack has damaged important energy facilities".
It said the company was working to restore electricity but the task was "complicated by repeated attacks".
Ukrainian President Volodymyr previously accused Russia of ramping up attacks on Ukraine ahead of trilateral talks next week with Russia.
In another strike, a Russian drone hit "a critical infrastructure facility" in the northeastern Kharkiv region, the mayor of Zlatopil city, Mykola Baksheyev, said on social media.
"Nearly 250,000 customers in the Kharkiv region were left without power," Baksheyev said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the night-time strikes had triggered "widespread power outages across the country".
"In the Zhytomyr region alone, 140 apartment buildings were left without heating following a Russian strike," he said, as temperatures in Ukraine already hovered around freezing.
He also said Russia had launched a drone at Komyshuvakha, a village in the Zaporizhzhia region where Moscow had hit an aid distribution centre on Monday in one of the deadliest attacks of the war.
The death toll has risen to 55 people, Zelenskyy said. Emergency services previously put it at 50 killed.
"This morning, the Russians attacked Komyshuvakha with an FPV drone, where emergency rescue operations have been underway for seven days ... Unfortunately, more people may still be under the rubble," Zelenskyy said.
The strikes came a day after Ukraine's energy ministry said a massive attack on energy facilities had plunged residents in five regions into darkness and significantly hampered electricity transmission in Kyiv.

articles.title_orig: A desert stirs to life: Chile's Atacama erupts in its biggest floral display in decades
articles.title_zh: A desert stirs to life: Chile's Atacama erupts in its biggest floral display in decades
articles.content_orig:
A field of colorful wildflowers blankets the Atacama Desert in northern Chile, transforming the world's driest non-polar desert into a vibrant landscape during the rare flowering desert phenomenon, known locally as the Desierto Florido, or Desert Bloom. Tamara Merino for NPR hide caption
COPIAPÓ, Chile — A vast swathe of Chile's Atacama Desert is now a patchwork of pinks, yellows, lilacs and purples stretching across the craggy desert floor as far as the eye can see.
This winter, heavy rains brought by the El Niño super cycle caused flash floods in the Atacama Desert, with some areas receiving the heaviest rainfall since records began in the 1950s.
Floodwaters in July and August destroyed or damaged dozens of homes,  forcing hundreds of people to evacuate.
A field of wildflowers blooms across Chile's Atacama Desert during the rare flowering phenomenon known as Desierto Florido, or Desert Bloom, triggered by unusually heavy rainfall that awakens dormant seeds. The brief blooms transform the world's driest nonpolar desert into a landscape of pink, purple, yellow and white. Huasco, Chile, Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. Tamara Merino for NPR hide caption
But the floral bloom that followed has been the largest and most colorful in 30 years — and perhaps ever.
The rainwater penetrated deeper into the parched ground than it has in decades, allowing millions of seeds, bulbs and tubers to sprout above the surface. Many had lain dormant for decades under the sand.
More than 200 species are in flower. A month ago, the first plants to emerge created a pale-yellow haze. This was followed by a soft purple hue as other bulbs germinated. Now, almost every indentation and crevice in the desert is streaked with color.
Scientists studying the phenomenon say there are patches of desert in bloom where flowers have never previously been recorded, suggesting that bulbs have remained dormant there since before the phenomenon was first studied in detail in 1997.
Moisés Grimberg has served as the administrator of Llanos de Challe National Park for the past three years and has worked in protected area management for 18 years. His work focuses on protecting the flora, fauna, and fragile ecosystems of the coastal desert near Huasco, Chile, while also managing the influx of tourists during the rare flowering desert phenomenon, known locally as the Desierto Florido. Huasco, Chile, on Monday October 19, 2026. Tamara Merino for NPR. Tamera Merino for NPR hide caption
"This is a natural seed bank, a dormant archive that becomes a living one with the rains," says Moisés Grimberg, the administrator of Llanos de Challe National Park.
"But it's a race against time — this brief biological window allows these species to complete their life cycle, which lasts roughly two to three months."
Llanos de Challe is a 113,000-acre national park along the arid coastline, where waves lap at pristine white sand beaches.
Grimberg says the park normally receives about 10,000 visitors a year. But with the desert in bloom, 15,000 tourists have visited over the last few weeks alone.
Across the desert, the roads are lined with tourists' cars. According to Chile's national tourism board, the region is expected to see around 300,000 overnight trips during the two months the desert is in bloom.
Among the star attractions are the nectar-filled, crimson flowers of the garra de león, with their long tails of flame-like green leaves. This endemic flower is coaxed out of dormancy by the rains and grows along just a few miles of this stretch of coastline in the Atacama Desert — nowhere else in the world.
A Garra de León flower blooms in the Atacama Desert of northern Chile during the rare flowering desert phenomenon, known locally as the Desierto Florido. This striking native flower is known for its vibrant red petals and is one of the region's rare and emblematic desert species. Canto del Agua, Chile, on Tuesday October 20, 2026. Tamara Merino for NPR. Tamera Merino for NPR hide caption
This bloom occurs every few years in what is the driest nonpolar desert on Earth. But scientists say the phenomenon is becoming more frequent as changes in the climate bring unseasonal rains.
The phenomenon gives rise to a thriving, transient ecosystem, with insects hatching and attracting lizards and bats, as well as larger mammals such as the guanaco.
A guanaco stands amid a carpet of Malvilla and Pata de Guanaco wildflowers during the rare flowering desert phenomenon, known locally as the Desierto Florido, in the Atacama Desert of northern Chile. Canto del Agua, Chile, on Tuesday October 20, 2026. Tamara Merino for NPR hide caption
Biologists from INIA, Chile's national seed bank, are collecting specimens to analyze in their laboratory before the brief flowering season ends.
"It's very exciting," said Ana Sandoval as she delicately shook seeds free from their casings to take back to INIA's taxonomist at its base in northern Chile.
"It's as if the desert is awakening. Sometimes people think it's an empty, arid place, devoid of life, but actually our desert is just waiting for the right conditions, and any precipitation, to awaken it."
The seed bank wants to preserve the genetic material and unique adaptations each plant has developed to survive the extreme, arid conditions.
Sandoval points out different ways plants harvest water as she walks. Some leaves are covered in fine hairs; others have a thick waxy cuticle.
A national park dedicated to the desert bloom was created in June 2023 to protect a 141,000-acre area where flowers spring up every few years. Now local authorities want to go further.
A cactus, which survives year-round despite the desert's extreme temperatures, stands amid a carpet of Malvilla and Pata de Guanaco wildflowers during the rare flowering desert phenomenon, known locally as the Desierto Florido, in the Atacama Desert of northern Chile. Canto del Agua, Chile. Tamara Merino for NPR hide caption
Miguel Vargas, the governor of the Atacama region, is beginning the process of seeking UNESCO World Heritage recognition for the desert bloom phenomenon.
"This represents a tremendous opportunity to strengthen special interest tourism and diversify our regional economy, which is currently heavily reliant on mining," he said. "Receiving UNESCO recognition would put the Atacama region on the world stage."
A couple of tourists visits the Atacama Desert during the rare flowering desert phenomenon, known locally as the Desierto Florido, in northern Chile. Huasco, Chile, on Monday October 19, 2026. Tamara Merino for NPR hide caption
Vargas hopes this will become Chile's eighth World Heritage site within a couple of years.
This year, the bloom is projected to last until mid-November.
As the flowers begin to fade, scientists will be left with two tantalising questions: was this the Atacama Desert's largest flowering event on record, and might closer examination reveal any previously unknown species among the millions of plants?

articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
I come to you today as a humble servant of the business and investing world with both good and bad news.
First, the sprinkles of good news, because I think we can agree we need something uplifting after watching the market get torched, blown up, and shredded to pieces in the aftermath of the blue wave .
Nothing changes in D.C. overnight, if at all. Companies' fundamentals are what will drive their stock prices in the long term. I don't think the fundamentals of companies have been destroyed this week, at least not to the extent that would warrant some of the sell-offs we witnessed.
A Hut 8 ( HUT ) data center build-out isn't getting a work order stoppage today that will derail the fourth quarter numbers. Dems aren't carting off AI data center C-suites to jail and sending their companies into bankruptcy.
Texas governor-elect Hinojosa isn't sending construction crews to data centers under an order to tear them all down and turn the land into parks. Elon Musk's SpaceX ( SPCX ) — based in Texas — is still operational this weekend, from what I can tell. Musk is still on pace to churn out Tesla ( TSLA ) robotaxis and robots in large numbers in 2027.
AMD ( AMD ) didn't offer a huge 2027 outlook this week on its earnings call because it fears a blue wave stopping its CPU momentum in its tracks.
In fact, AMD CEO Lisa Su told me the demand she is seeing is off the charts !
Hilton ( HLT ) CEO Chris Nassetta is so confident in his business trends that he told me this week he felt compelled to share directional guidance for 2027 with investors. Nassetta normally doesn't share these types of year-ahead specifics.
"Here's the reality. Our political system has been built pretty well," Nassetta said on Sozzi Unleashed . "Our founders did a pretty good job of creating a resilient system. We always figure it out. We'll figure it out this time. The reality is, in the next two or three years, I don't see any real dramatic impact as a result of the last couple days."
Nassetta is going on year 20 as CEO of Hilton, an almost unheard-of run in the C-suite. I don't think you get to log 20 years as Hilton CEO if you are wrong on a lot of stuff — and I think Chris makes a valid point on the political winds that are always blowing.
Now the bad news — and it's short and to the point.
We can no longer believe earnings estimates for 2027 and 2028. While in one breath I'm telling you corporate fundamentals haven't been destroyed this week, in the other breath I acknowledge they have taken a minor hit.
Data center projects won't come to a screeching halt in the US. It will just take a higher bar to get them built. And it will be costlier to get the deals done.
This was a surprise factor to the earnings estimates for the AI ecosystem, and that's what the market is adjusting to.
Should the selling in markets persist, it could be a surprise factor to the industrial companies supporting the AI boom — for example, Caterpillar ( CAT ) dump trucks. And from there, we get into the economic damage from a more restricted AI boom.
I am making a lot of assumptions here.
But will leave you with this: The world didn't end this week.
This is not the dot-com bust.
This is an adjustment period, and soon it'll be a period where you can no longer ignore the historically cheap valuations on names like Nvidia ( NVDA ), Micron, and Sandisk.

The president of the Canary Islands has announced that Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has agreed to convene an emergency meeting of the Interministerial Commission on Immigration on Tuesday to address the growing pressure facing the island of El Hierro following a recent surge in migrant arrivals.
Fernando Clavijo said he had briefed the prime minister on the severity of the situation on the island and the mounting discontent among residents.
The El Hierro Island Council has declared a social emergency following the arrival of more than 8,000 migrants over the last five weeks.
Between 1 and 6 November, 49 boats carrying a total of 4,587 migrants arrived in the Canary Islands, according to the regional government.
Of these, 35 reached El Hierro, where authorities say the pressure on local resources is "extraordinary."
Clavijo said the Canary Islands have been calling for months for additional resources, better planning and a coordinated governmental response to deal with the situation.
"This meeting must serve to agree, between both governments and the relevant ministries, on a joint action plan, with specific, responsible measures and deadlines for implementation," Clavijo wrote in a post on social media. "We cannot continue to act only when the situation worsens."
He said he had also requested "urgent meetings" with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen as well as European Commissioner for Internal Affairs and Migration, Magnus Brunner.
"The Canary Islands cannot continue to face, practically on their own, a situation that requires the involvement of the Spanish government and Europe," Clavijo added.

articles.title_zh: Vinted and eBay could be included in under-16 social media ban, minister says
articles.content_orig:
Vinted and eBay could be included in the list of platforms set to be banned for under-16s, the culture secretary has said.
Lisa Nandy said the government was "looking seriously" at including the retailing websites in the social media ban "in order to keep children safe".
The UK's social media ban for those under the age of 16 is set to come into force in March next year, with children barred from accessing platforms such as Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat.
In response, eBay said it was looking forward to "understanding more and continuing to work constructively with the government". Vinted has not responded to requests for comment.
Asked on the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg if the government was looking to ban under-16s from Vinted and eBay, Nandy said: "We are looking seriously at doing so in order to keep children safe."
It came after the Sunday Times reported that the UK's social media ban was being expanded to include the platforms, which are popular for selling second-hand goods.
The newspaper said the move was over fears that messaging functions allowed strangers to groom children. It suggested similar reselling platforms, Depop and Facebook Marketplace, would also be included in the list of banned sites.
Businesses and individuals sell a host of goods on eBay, which has been a major global player in the online reselling market for years. The platform states on its website that it currently requires all of its members to be over 18 years old because listings involve "entering into a contract".
Vinted also says its users need to be at least 18 years old. The site, which mostly sees users buy and sell unwanted clothes and other fashion items, has grown rapidly in recent times to reach 17 million UK users.
An eBay spokesperson said the company was "focused on providing a trusted and safe marketplace experience for our millions of customers".
"While the details of the proposed legislation are not yet clear, we look forward to understanding more and continuing to work constructively with the government," they added in a statement.
The government announced it would ban under-16s accessing social media in June this year, with children prevented from accessing 10 of the biggest platforms.
YouTube will also be banned for under-16s, but YouTube Kids - a version of the video-sharing app designed to be safe for children - will not be included.
A complete list of affected platforms has not yet been released, but the government said it would cover those "whose purpose is to enable social interaction and which allow users to post material".
That means platforms which have livestreaming or features that enable the potential for strangers to contact children will also be restricted, which includes gaming sites.
It does not mean that Roblox, the biggest gaming site in the UK for eight to 12-year-olds for example, will be banned for under-16s. However, certain features such as its chat function will be restricted.
The UK's ban comes after a similar one was introduced in Australia last year.
Many children there have found ways to get round it, but the UK has said it intends to take a tougher approach.
In recent weeks, attention has turned to how such a ban would be enforced.
Last month, the communications regulator Ofcom set out its recommendations for the most effective ways to identify which of the UK's millions of social media users are aged over 16.

articles.title_zh: DoorDash Shareholders Aren’t Convinced the Company Can Take On Amazon
articles.content_orig:
DoorDash employees might have to make fewer LinkedIn connections as a result of their employer's $17 billion deal to buy Instacart.
The food-delivery service told employees as much in an internal question-and-answer document filed with the SEC on Thursday.
"Can I connect with Instacart employees on LinkedIn?" reads one of the questions in the document.
"Not at this time," the answer says. "Please do not request any new connections with any Instacart employees on LinkedIn, even if you have a prior relationship."
The guidance shows that a pending takeover can change life inside the companies involved, sometimes for long periods. Merging companies must remain independent competitors, limiting employees' ability to coordinate or share sensitive information.
The document tells employees not to accept LinkedIn connection requests from Instacart employees, and that the two companies must continue to operate separately until the deal closes. DoorDash and Instacart said they expect the purchase to close either at the end of 2027 or in the first half of 2028.
Companies planning a merger or acquisition will often take steps to prevent employees from engaging in so-called gun-jumping, or behaving as if the deal is already done, something that could thwart the deal before it's completed. This might include sharing competitively sensitive information, coordinating on pricing or bidding, or discussing jobs with people at the other company without authorization.
"You're supposed to continue to act like independent competitors until the deal closes," said David Gelfand, senior counsel specializing in antitrust law at Cleary Gottlieb, and former deputy assistant attorney general for litigation in the antitrust division of the US Department of Justice.
By asking employees to refrain from certain LinkedIn connections, the companies could be trying to prevent brain drain, said Chris Selland, a lecturer at Northeastern University's D'Amore-McKim School of Business.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
DoorDash and Instacart already compete in the same industry. Discussions between employees could lead one company to hire employees from the other — bringing valuable connections, such as customer contacts, with them. "That could blow up the whole agreement," he said.
However, several M&A experts told Business Insider they'd never heard of employees at companies undergoing a deal being barred from connecting on LinkedIn or any other social media platform.
DoorDash declined to comment.
Whether Instacart and DoorDash are acting sensibly, or imposing an overly broad restriction on ordinary employee behavior is "a great antitrust examination question," said William Kovacic, a former FTC chairman and the director of George Washington University's Competition Law Center.

articles.title_orig: New Zealand dairy giant Fonterra speeds up China innovation
articles.title_zh: New Zealand dairy giant Fonterra speeds up China innovation
articles.content_orig:
Fonterra Co-operative Group Ltd is accelerating product development with Chinese customers as the New Zealand dairy giant seeks to capture growing demand for protein-rich foods and dairy products tailored to local tastes.
The company is leveraging its six application centers in China to help bakeries, beverage chains and food manufacturers bring new products to market faster, supported by investments in production capacity in New Zealand, CEO Richard Allen said in an interview during the China International Import Expo in Shanghai.
"We know how fast the China market moves and how quickly trends change," Allen said. "Alongside our customers, we can work with them to create new products with new selling points."
A recent visit to Chengdu, Sichuan province, highlighted how much the market had evolved since he worked in China's foodservice sector many years ago.
Allen said dairy products had become more prominent in bakeries, supermarkets and membership stores, with a growing number of products emphasizing their protein content.
Chinese food and beverage brands are also increasingly highlighting the grass-fed origins of New Zealand dairy ingredients to differentiate their products and strengthen their premium positioning.
However, turning those attributes into sales requires products that deliver both quality and value.
Fonterra works with customers to select ingredients that meet nutritional and taste requirements while keeping costs affordable for consumers and commercially viable for producers, Allen said.
"You've got to have nutrition, but it also has to taste good," he said.
Its six application centers in China bring together chefs, marketing specialists and sales teams to develop products suited to local and regional tastes.
For one bakery customer, Fonterra explored incorporating Sichuan's signature mala, or spicy and numbing, flavors into baked goods. Allen also cited the pairing of Anchor butter with pineapple buns as an example of how dairy ingredients can be incorporated into established local food traditions.
"By being on the ground, close to our customers, to their consumers, it allows us to work every day with our customers on developing new products very quickly," he said.
China is also becoming a source of product innovation for Fonterra's operations elsewhere in Asia.
Dairy-topped tea drinks developed in China, for example, have created opportunities among the company's foodservice customers in Southeast Asia, Allen said.
Meanwhile, the overseas expansion of Chinese restaurant and beverage chains is opening another avenue for growth.
As these brands enter international markets, they increasingly seek consistent supplies of familiar ingredients to maintain product quality and taste across their global operations.
Fonterra is supporting Chinese customers expanding into Southeast Asia, the United States, Europe, Australia and New Zealand, drawing on its international supply network and foodservice expertise.
"Not only can we support our local customers in other markets, but we can support Chinese brands in accessing other markets," Allen said.
The strategy builds on Fonterra's established ingredients and foodservice businesses in China, where the cooperative has operated for nearly five decades.
Allen described China as one of Fonterra's cornerstone markets, with demand for dairy ingredients and nutritional products continuing to create opportunities for long-term growth.
To support that demand, Fonterra is investing NZ$150 million ($87 million) to expand ultra-high-temperature cream production at its Edendale facility in New Zealand.
The additional capacity will serve customers in China and other markets, complementing investments in local application centers and culinary, marketing and sales teams.
The expansion comes as Fonterra reported stronger financial results for the year ended July 2026. The cooperative posted revenue of NZ$27 billion and total group operating profit of NZ$3.4 billion in results released on Sept 24.
Fonterra has also announced an additional NZ$1 billion investment over three years to expand its protein manufacturing network in New Zealand's South Island and improve environmental performance.
In China, Allen sees further opportunities in protein-rich products. During his visits to Chinese supermarkets, he was struck by the growing number of products promoting their protein content.
"For us, being agile and moving fast, and ensuring our customers are agile and moving fast, is about being close to the market and really understanding what's happening," Allen said.

China has confirmed that it is discussing a historic meeting of Xi Jinping , Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump .
Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said at a press briefing this week that Beijing was “in communication with relevant parties regarding a meeting between the three heads of state” .
The three-leader gathering could take place this month on the sidelines of a regional summit in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen .
It would be historic if the meeting were to happen, but experts argued the leaders of China, Russia and the US were unlikely to discuss anything substantive because their interests were at odds. They would gather for a photo, the experts said, with China carefully choreographing the meeting .
“I think it will happen. The question is the format and the content,” Sun Yun, director of the Stimson Centre’s China programme, said. “China wants the image but not the costs.”
Beijing is hosting this year’s summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, a 21-member grouping that includes the US and Russia, this month.
Mr Trump is expected to travel to Shenzhen and meet the Chinese leader for the third time this year, maintaining a fragile trade truce that is set to expire in January.
In a sign that tensions persist, American trade representative Jamieson Greer urged China during a video call with vice premier He Lifeng on Friday to take “concrete actions to fully implement its past commitments, particularly as they relate to agricultural purchases, rare earths, and critical minerals”.
Chinese news agency Xinhua reported on Saturday that the two sides had constructive exchanges and that Beijing expressed concerns about Washington’s restrictive economic and trade measures against it.
Mr Trump previously said that he would be interested in meeting Mr Xi and Mr Putin to discuss nuclear arms controls, though Mr Putin was focused on talking about the Ukraine war without Kyiv at the table.
“Putin has the most to gain from a leaders’ trilateral and the Russians are clearly behind the push for a meeting, which would be a diplomatic coup,” said Danny Russel, a former senior US State Department official who served in former president Barack Obama ’s administration.
Mr Trump, with his “crush on authoritarian strongmen", would love the meeting, though he clearly had been warned by his advisers to steer clear of Ukraine as a topic of the discussions, said Mr Russel.
Ms Sun of the Stimson Centre said Russia would likely use the summit to nudge China and the US closer to Moscow's positions on Ukraine, while “China will have to manage Russian manipulation”.
China also would not engage in talks on arms controls or discussions about Ukraine or Iran, other than its diplomatic refrain that peace was important and wars should end, Ms Sun said.
Beijing's biggest challenge might be the perception. The summit “should not be equated to three great powers dividing up the world”, she said.
The meeting might amount to no more than a photo opportunity that would allow Mr Putin to be seen next to American and Chinese leaders, Craig Singleton, senior director of the China programme at the Foundation for Defence of Democracies, said.
“But these photo opportunities have diminishing diplomatic returns,” Mr Singleton said. “The spectacle may be historic without producing anything particularly consequential.”

articles.title_orig: 'We were inseparable': How imaginary friends help us in real life
articles.title_zh: 'We were inseparable': How imaginary friends help us in real life
articles.content_orig:
From invisible ballerinas to chatty milk cartons, the benefits of made-up friends can last well into adulthood and help us master tricky real-life situations.
Throughout my childhood I had many great friendships, but one group truly left a mark. Capin, Mia and Hannah were my closest friends from an early age, and I recall lots of happy memories together. On hot summer days we would spend hours making daisy chains, spotting peculiar-shaped clouds as they blotted out the Sun's rays, baking fairy cakes, playing hide and seek, practising handstands, cartwheels – exerting ourselves day in and day out until summer drew to an end.
We were an inseparable foursome, yet not the conventional type: Capin, Mia and Hannah were a complete figment of my imagination.
They were my imaginary friends who I shared secrets with, looked to for guidance and turned to when I needed a good dose of fun. But I didn't create them because I was lonely or shy or lacking in real-life friends. In fact, all these years later I'm still not sure where they came from or why.
Whatever my friends' origin, research on imaginary friends suggests that I was lucky to have them. From chatty milk cartons to multi-coloured alligators and a magical ghost giraffe, studies reveal a dazzling range of imaginary creatures accompanying children through the ups and downs of childhood. There's emerging evidence that these have wide-ranging benefits, including enhanced empathy and creativity, which can last well into adulthood.
By the time they are seven years old , two-thirds of children have had an imaginary friend, a character created by them which they interact with or talk about on a regular basis, according to psychologists Naomi Aguiar and Marjorie Taylor.
"These children don't have fewer friends than other children, they have the same number of reciprocal friendships as kids without imaginary friends. And the reality of what the data shows is that they're just like other kids in almost every respect," says Aguiar, a psychologist and the author of Imaginary Friends and the People who Create Them . She currently researches online learning and child relationships with imaginary friends and AI chatbots at Oregon State University in the US.
Often, children's imaginary friends appear when there are no others around, according to Aguiar – not as a sign of deep loneliness, but just because in that specific moment, the child happens to be alone and would like some company.
"A lot of children create imaginary friends because they're fun and because they really like social interactions. So, if there's no social partner to interact with [in a given situation], they create an imaginary friend," says Aguiar.
But these made-up beings can have benefits far beyond just providing company, research suggests. Children with imaginary friends may excel at being creative storytellers, can be less shy, are more interested in fantasy, better able to focus their attention, use screens less and may have more vivid mental imagery than children without imaginary friendships.
Each imaginary friend is unique to its child creator and is often customised to match the ever-shifting whims and needs which appear throughout childhood, Aguiar explains.
One of her favourite examples is the case of a girl who had an invisible milk carton as a friend. What the girl loved about the milk carton was that it wasn't human, and so the milk carton taught her about what it was like to not be human, and she taught the milk carton about what it was like to be human, Aguiar says.
My own imaginary friends appeared when I was around three years old. Hannah and Mia were inspired by two girls from a ballet film. They never walked, only jumped, leapt and spun in a constant cycle of ballet sequences, and they wore matching soft pink leotards, tutus and ballet slippers. But Capin, he truly was an enigma – I have no idea where he came from.
Capin was older than the three of us. He had dark hair which covered his eyes, and an air of sophistication that materialised in a grey cloud which trailed after him. He often hung back from the three of us, offering tidbits of knowledge when needed. Where the girls delighted me with their impressive allegros and pliés, Capin's thoughtful advice was a constant comfort.
Despite their differences, their abilities to entertain were the same. In the winter months we would paint, colour, glue and stick everything in sight. Draw faces on foggy, moisture slick windows, marvel at the explosions of colour which splattered the inky sky every November, flick through catalogues and circle gifts we hoped would come down the chimney on Christmas Day.
"The most important part of an imaginary companion for me is the creation of the mind and interacting with that mind," says Paige Davis, associate professor of developmental psychology and psychopathology at the University of Leeds, in the UK. Some are based upon real-life people or personified objects, and some materialise in the form of an animal or fantastical creature.
Marta Giménez-Dasí at the University of Valencia in Spain and her colleagues found that children aged four to six years old who had imaginary friends scored higher than children without imaginary friends in assessments of theory of mind and emotional understanding – meaning they were able to understand people have beliefs, desires and intentions which differ from their own.
It's not clear whether this emotional understanding is a result of cultivating imaginary companions – or if it's the other way round, and children who are interested in others' minds, are more likely to create companions.
Davis and her colleagues investigated whether the benefits of having imaginary friends extended beyond neurotypical children.
Autistic children make and maintain successful friendships, yet their approach to communication, social understanding and emotional understanding, is often different to their neurotypical peers, which can have an impact on relationships, Davis says. Also, they often indulge in imaginative play a little differently, usually engaging in imaginative activities such as drawing instead of make-believe, says Davis. Together, this suggests they may have less inclination to create imaginary friends.
However, when Davis interviewed the parents of 124 autistic children she found that 49% of participants reported their child had created an imaginary friend between the ages of one and 11 years old.
Through these companionships, children with autism create an opportunity to practice social interactions, which they may find challenging, experts say. "One of the struggles of autism is understanding and navigating social relationships, and creating an imaginary companion can be a risk-free forum for exploring," says Tracy Gleason, professor of psychology at Wellesley College in the US.
Consistent, repeated conversations and interactions with an invisible entity which has, in a way, its own mind and helps give an autistic child a foundational understanding of social interactions, which they may find useful, according to Davis and Gleason.
"The parents of autistic children who created an imaginary friend reported they felt their child had better theory of mind than parents of those without one," says Davis. "And the ones that created imaginary friends also had significantly more interest spending time or making new friends."
While they can encourage children to form real-life relationships, imaginary friendships also provide children with a safe space to navigate social complexities, Davis, Gleason and Aguiar say. They can help children begin to develop their boundaries, understand their comfort levels, learn how to navigate difficult conversations and establish common ground to work through a problem.

articles.title_zh: Italy's Meloni blames pro-Russian hackers for leaking foreign minister's personal data to dark web
articles.content_orig:
Italy's prime minister blamed pro-Russian hackers for leaking the country's foreign minister's data onto the dark web.
Italian foreign minister Antonio Tajani said on Saturday he has been subjected to intimidation and that his personal data was leaked because of his support for Ukraine, but did not specify who was behind it.
In a post on X, Tajani blamed "cybercriminals" for posting his personal data on the dark web, a term used to describe a section of the internet only accessible with specialist software, commonly associated with criminal activities.
In a separate statement on Saturday, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni blamed "pro-Russian hackers" for the leaks.
Meloni expressed her "full solidarity" with the foreign minister over "what has come to light regarding the activities of pro-Russian hackers and the dissemination of personal data relating to him on the dark web."
"The sale of confidential information about institutional representatives is a cause of serious concern and must be tackled with the utmost determination," Meloni added.
Tajani said the leaks have been going for days and expose him to threats and intimidation. He added that his family have also been targeted and the perpetrators are still looking for more information.
"Our position on Ukraine is the political reason I have been targeted," the minister said. "Defending the freedom of a sovereign state, taking a clear stand in support of a nation's democracy and independence, is dangerous for these criminal entities."
Tajani said he would not be intimidated by the incident and vowed to continue his support of Italian allies.
"I will continue working to defend my ministry and Italy, and I will keep strengthening ties and cooperation with our allies so that we can protect ourselves together," the minister said.
